<reason>Side B won a close, high-quality exchange. B's opening reframed the motion as wealth tax vs. targeted reforms that reach untaxed gains, and that comparison frame held up all debate. B consistently exposed internal tensions in A's case: deferral-with-interest undercuts A's objection to delayed collection; "wealth cannot hide" sits awkwardly beside conceded valuation friction; and the two-investor/losing-business objection was never answered beyond A's "rough justice" concession. B also defused A's best pressure—the political-feasibility asymmetry—by noting both paths need legislation, that statutory exemptions do not expire annually just because assessment does, and that A's wealth tax equally rests on promises of good design. A's answers to pressure were direct and well-formatted, and A's rhetoric ("tax the thing that stays," "friction vs. invisibility") was the more memorable, but the persistence-of-the-base claim was weakened by B's point that taxable ownership, not physical assets, is what matters. A also paid a small execution cost with a clipped opening. On substance, B made the debate easier to decide by holding the burden A never fully discharged: justifying annual taxation of already-taxed principal beyond what death-time taxation of gains achieves.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 ([B2.1]-[B2.7]) was the decisive exchange: it broke A's "death tax concedes the principle" move by distinguishing taxing untaxed appreciation from repeatedly taxing principal, and reframed A's "rough justice" as an unaddressed fairness failure—damage A never fully repaired in later rounds.</best_rebuttal>
